view: Ibn ʿAṭiyya abridges conflicting narrative versions and retains details he considers sounder and needed for the verse.
The cave story appears in many detailed transmissions from early historians and exegetes.
Transmitted accounts diverge on dates, rulers, lineage, appearances, names, and the identity of the People of the Inscription.
The story's wide circulation among Christians and the People of the Book led communities to reshape its details.
Muslim compilers also gathered outside accounts through converts such as Wahb and Kaʿb, and later transmitters sometimes treated them as Prophetic.
Most historians place the story between Jesus and Muḥammad; it is absent from the two Testaments, though Christian accounts preserve it extensively.
Christian versions resemble some Muslim accounts but differ on the number of sleepers, the dog, and the length of sleep.
The Qurʾān selects the story's guiding lessons rather than furnishing a complete historical record.
The Cave and Dhū l-Qarnayn stories frame the sūra as primary themes.
The Qurʾānic story moves from the youths' withdrawal and sleep to their awakening, discovery, and a mosque at their cave.
“Thus” may compare the revival with itself to heighten wonder.
“Thus” compares the awakening with God's earlier making or preserving them asleep; both are signs of divine power.
Baʿth originally means stirring something up; it also denotes dispatching messengers or raising the dead.
An Arabic poem uses baʿath for waking young men at dawn.
The youths awoke with their bodies, clothes, or condition preserved despite the long sleep.
A shepherd opened the cave while sheltering sheep from rain; the youths awoke the next morning and sent one with old silver.
When the envoy led the king and people to the cave, terror kept them from entering; a church or mosque was later built there.
ʿIkrima reports that Christian royal youths slept until a believing king and community arose amid disagreement over bodily resurrection.
The ancient coin disclosed the sleepers' era and the king presented them as proof that body and soul rise together.
A report says visitors found the sleepers' bodies without souls, and the king called them a sign of God.
Ibn ʿAbbās reported that the sleepers' bones had vanished more than three centuries later.
Ibn Isḥāq places the awakening under the righteous king Theodosius, who ruled for sixty eight years while his people disputed the Hour.
Some denied bodily resurrection and said only souls would rise; falsehood gained over the believers.
Theodosius wore sackcloth, sat on ashes, and prayed for a sign to settle the dispute.
God displayed the sleepers to confirm the Hour and bodily resurrection, answer the king's prayer, and unite believers.
God inspired Olyas to clear stones from the cave for a sheep pen; the youths revived, greeted one another, and prayed, while fear kept others away.
The envoy returned with the townspeople, and the youths understood their awakening was a sign of resurrection.
A report says Muḥammad asked to see the sleepers but was directed to send four companions with his greeting and invitation to faith.
Gabriel told Muḥammad to place Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿAlī, and Abū Dharr on a cloth and summon Solomon's wind, which carried them to the cave.
The dog greeted the four companions; God restored the youths' souls, and they accepted Muḥammad's message before sleeping again until the end.
A variant says the Mahdi will greet the youths, who will be revived and then sleep until resurrection.
The Prophet prayed to remain with loved ones and asked forgiveness for those loving him and his household.
After a tyrant died, a righteous king ruled; the youths awoke and disagreed whether they slept one day, two days, or longer.
A saying attributed to ʿAlī states that people are asleep and awaken when they die.
A report says they entered with a dog and slept until the king and city disappeared, then awoke in a new era.
After the envoy rejoined them, the youths returned to deep sleep and were later found perfectly preserved by the king and townspeople.
God awakened the youths from their long sleep, which resembled death.
Their awakening displays God's power over sleep, death, and bodily resurrection and strengthens certainty or gratitude.
The awakening first enabled the sleepers to understand their own condition, a fundamental human concern.
The sleepers' story answers Quraysh's question drawn from Jewish informants; their response to the sign tests whether they will believe.
The youths' despair over coercive falsehood parallels the man revived after a century; their awakening shows time cannot erase truth.
Awakening is the first spiritual wakefulness that makes latent realities of the soul available for discussion and fulfillment.
Awakening symbolizes the return to sobriety after spiritual intoxication.
The lām marks the questioning as an outcome or consequence of the awakening, rather than its ultimate purpose.
note: Disagreement turns on whether the lām states God's immediate purpose or the outcome of a larger sign.

view: The Qurʾān first summarizes and then recounts the sleepers' exchange in fuller detail.
The city to which they sent the envoy was Ephesus, their former home.
note: Other reports name Ephesus or Daqsus; several identify Ephesus as Tarsus's former name.

view: The city is identified as Tarsus, said in some reports to have been called Ephesus before Islam.
note: Other reports name Ephesus or Daqsus; several identify Ephesus as Tarsus's former name.

view: The city is named Daqsus or Daphsus, sometimes identified with present day Tarsus.
note: Other reports name Ephesus or Daqsus; several identify Ephesus as Tarsus's former name.

view: The envoy saw Christian signs and heard Jesus invoked openly in a city once hostile to them, leaving him bewildered.
The envoy learned the city was Ephesus yet feared he had lost his mind and tried to leave unseen.
Townspeople told the envoy Deqianus had died long ago, and he realized centuries had passed.
A saying calls Muḥammad the city of knowledge and ʿAlī its gate.
Tarsus, said to have been Ephesus, is described as fertile and formerly Armenian before Muslim rule.
Rujayb near Amman is favored as the cave on archaeological signs and some Muslim reports.
note: The author favors Rujayb yet says none of the proposed sites is proven.

view: Amman occupies ancient Philadelphia, a Roman city before Islam.
Proposed caves include sites near Damascus, Petra, Scandinavia, and Nakhchivan.
No proposed cave is conclusively identified; northern European and Caucasus sites conflict with the story's Roman setting.
note: The author favors Rujayb yet says none of the proposed sites is proven.

view: The mutual questioning was an intended purpose of the awakening, opening the wisdoms of the episode.
note: Disagreement turns on whether the lām states God's immediate purpose or the outcome of a larger sign.

view: The youths questioned one another about how long they had stayed.
Their mutual questioning was meant to disclose God's power and increase reflection, knowledge, certainty, or gratitude.
The introductory qāla resumes the narrative and explains how their mutual questioning occurred.
The questioner was their leader or eldest companion, Maksalmina or Miksalmina.
The questioner was Yamlikha or Tamlikha, the companion who managed their provisions.
The questioner may have been anxious about having missed a prayer.
The questioner sensed an unusually long sleep from their condition or other signs.
The singular questioner and two plural replies imply at least seven youths.
Kam asks how many days they had stayed, with “days” omitted; it is accusative with labithtum.
Kam is adverbial here, with “days” omitted and supplied by the answer.
Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, and ʿĀṣim articulate thāʾ distinctly in forms of labithtum; four other readers assimilate it.
The assimilated pronunciation of labithtum is permitted because the articulation points are close.
“A day” can denote slightly more than a night and a day; observed sun and shadow cannot establish a precise full day.
Their grown hair and nails suggested that their sleep had lasted longer than their first estimate.
After prayer, the youths questioned Yemliha; he thought Deqianus still pursued them and threatened sacrifice or death.
The youths believed they had slept only their usual night and did not know 309 years had passed.
A report says the youths awoke hungry under a Muslim king, estimated their sleep as a day or less, deferred to God, and sent one with old coins.
A report from Ibn ʿAbbās says one youth estimated a day and another about a day; their leader warned that disagreement brings ruin.
The claim that some youths said two days or more is rejected as conflicting with the verse's day or part of one; disagreement over judgment is not blameworthy dissent.
They estimated a day or part of one because they entered the cave in the morning and awoke later with daylight still visible.
They first said a day, then revised it to part of a day after observing that the sun had not set.
note: Disagreement turns on whether aw expresses one uncertain answer, a correction, or answers from different speakers.

view: “A day or part of a day” expresses an uncertain estimate of elapsed time.
note: Disagreement turns on whether aw expresses one uncertain answer, a correction, or answers from different speakers.

view: The phrase may distribute two answers: some said a day and others part of a day.
note: Disagreement turns on whether aw expresses one uncertain answer, a correction, or answers from different speakers.

view: Sleep left them unable to measure the duration accurately from ordinary signs.
Their time and weather on waking likely resembled those at sleep onset, since a sharp change would have alerted them.
Awakening in the afternoon fits the proposed shopping trip better than awakening just before sunset, since the envoy needed daylight to return.
The story exposes the deceptiveness of humans' earthbound sense of time.
Worldly life passes like a brief dream, whose full truth is recognized at death or the world's end.
Their reasonable but mistaken estimate permits acting on probable judgment and does not count as lying.
Their brief estimate parallels how people after death or at resurrection will perceive a long interval as short, as in 2:259 and other verses.
The sleepers' question and answer parallel the revived man in 2:259 and point to God's power over life, death, and resurrection.
For a lover, even a long time with the beloved feels short because longing continues.
Absorption away from self kept the youths from noticing elapsed time or their condition.
The reading that one person said both the first estimate and “your Lord knows best” is rejected as ill fitting the dialogue's two groups.
Their eldest leader Maksalmina gave the reply that God knew best.
Their leader Yamlikha or Tamlikha gave the reply that God knew best.
A second group of youths corrected the first estimate by saying God knew best.
The group as a whole may have deferred the duration to God after discussing it.
The words that their Lord knows best may be God's own statement rather than the youths' reply.
Maksalimina urged his companions to accept death rather than abandon faith in God and the afterlife.
They stopped estimating and entrusted the exact duration of their stay to God.
Their ending the disagreement in God's knowledge expresses mutual affection and fellowship in faith.
Some sleepers recognized that elapsed time has no independent reality in relation to death and resurrection, explaining the two viewpoints.
God alone knows the precise duration because He placed them in that state and directly encompasses events beyond human indicators.
The spiritually discerning group leaves duration to God and sends an envoy to the city for insight and completion.
In the agency report, saghiya denotes a man's adherents who incline toward him.
Aḥadukum means one from the group and avoids wāḥidukum's possible implication of a distinguished leader.
The commands can address either an unspecified delegate or a known companion whose name the narration omits.
The messenger sent to buy food was Yamlikha or Tamlikha.
Yemliha was sent secretly with old coins to learn city news and bring food; he saw that the cave entrance was unsealed.
Areus, Astius, and townspeople of every station accompanied the envoy to the cave.
A report describes ʿAbd al-Raḥmān and Umayya delegating protection of each other's dependents, with Umayya objecting to the name al-Raḥmān.
The Prophet sent Jābir to Khaybar to collect fifteen wasqs from his agent, giving a physical sign for identification.
The Prophet delegated repayment of a camel debt with a better camel, showing that a healthy present person may appoint agents.
They left an unknowable debate and turned to the more urgent task of obtaining food.
The youths sent one companion to town to purchase food for their hungry group.
The youths share religious insight, money, delegation, prudent advice, and concern for one another's safety.
Sending one youth to buy for the group supports the validity of appointing an agent.
Agency is valid for delegable lawful rights, but not for a usurper or an unlawful act.
All permit agency for a person with an excuse; most also permit a healthy present person to appoint an agent.
note: Disagreement concerns whether a healthy person present may appoint an agent without an excuse.

view: Abū Ḥanīfa and Saḥnūn disallow agency for a present person without excuse; al-Qurṭubī permits it, while Ibn al-ʿArabī suggests a concern about oppressors.
note: Disagreement concerns whether a healthy person present may appoint an agent without an excuse.

view: One envoy suffices because one person's perfected knowledge can awaken and teach the others.
Wariq means silver, whether minted into coins or unminted; it may serve as currency.
Wariq here refers specifically to silver coins or dirhams.
Riqqa, another name for silver, may derive from wariqa by dropping its initial wāw.
A different vocalization of waraq with fatḥa can mean camels or sheep, as a poem attests.
Al-Biqāʿī derives wariq and related forms from a root of gathering, associating silver's shape, beauty, and usefulness with livelihood.
The wariq lexical family is linked to foliage, worldly beauty, paper, animal life, blood, wealth, and contrasting degrees of human worth.
Related forms describe both returning empty handed and gaining much wealth.
The extended lexicon includes verdure, early pasture, a variegated wolf, and a flawed bow, connected by color or usefulness.
Related q-w-r forms include tiptoe stalking, circular cuts, compact terrain, spacious houses, and gathering or contraction; a proverb names the Qara tribe.
Bi-wariqikum is circumstantial to aḥadukum: the envoy goes carrying the silver.
“This” suggests that the coin was present or held out when the youths sent their companion.
The unusual emphasis “your silver, this” foreshadows how the coin's three century age would expose the youths.
Readers vary between kasra and sukūn on the rāʾ of wariqikum; sukūn eases pronunciation and both forms mean silver.
A variant puts kasra on the wāw of wariqikum; the form is rare or considered less preferred.
Some readers assimilate qāf into kāf in wariqikum; the articulation favors this direction.
Ibn Jinnī explains the reported qāf kāf assimilation as concealment, since true assimilation would transfer the qāf's vowel to rāʾ.
The kasra wāw, still rāʾ, assimilated qāf reading is challenged for bringing two consonants into sukūn together.
ʿAlī's reading bawāriqikum is a collective form relating to silver.
Abū Ḥayyān disputes al-Zamakhsharī's attribution of a kasra rāʾ and assimilated qāf form to Ibn Kathīr.
The report of ʿArfaja's foul smelling silver nose and its replacement with gold is cited to show that wariq can mean unminted silver.
Their old silver coins bore the image or stamp of the king from whose reign they had fled.
The ancient coin alerted the food seller or townspeople to the envoy's unusual age and exposed the sleepers' story.
An envoy took an ancient coin to Ephesus; its age exposed him, the ruler checked records, and people rejoiced at the youths' story.
Townspeople accused the envoy of hidden treasure, bound him, and paraded him as an unknown stranger.
The envoy was brought to two righteous governors, Areus and Astius, whom he feared were agents of Deqianus.
No one knew the envoy or his father; some called him mad and officials threatened torture over the ancient coin.
The envoy said he had entered Ephesus the previous evening, asked officials to meet his companions, and Areus saw a possible divine sign.
A coin from 309 years earlier brought the envoy to the believing king, whose archived tablet matched his story.
ʿĀʾisha advised a pilgrim in iḥrām about fastening a money belt to secure provisions.
Ibn ʿUmar cited the prohibition on taking two dates at once without a companion's permission as evidence concerning shared food.
Ibn ʿAbbās compared the sleepers' silver coins in size to the hooves of a young camel.
Al-Ālūsī dismisses a paper leaf interpretation tied to the silver nose report because the claim that silver rotted is unsound.
A report says the youths were money changers; al-Ṣādiq distinguishes verbal exchange from dealing in coins.
The envoy's ancient clothes and speech, as well as his coin, made him conspicuous.
The youths carried money and provisions with them when they fled, and some silver remained for the food errand.
The verse leaves the precise discovery route unstated; town inquiry may gradually have uncovered the sleepers' origins.
One view defines the elect's trust as abandoning ordinary causes, citing people who survived poison or extraordinary danger.
Carrying money or provisions and taking practical means to obtain food are compatible with trust in God.
Their shared money and food support pooling costs and eating together even when appetites differ.
The verse alone does not prove a partnership, since each youth might have given his money separately.
note: The contrary inference treats “your silver” as evidence of pooled funds.

view: The army of khabt report is inconclusive for pooled food because Abū ʿUbayda may have distributed equal portions.
The shared purse teaches companions to share resources and avoid habitual begging.
Silver symbolizes innate first principles that yield divine knowledge; the city is a gathering place or the city of knowledge whose gate is ʿAlī.
Falyanẓur can mean physical inspection or mental consideration.
The verb “look” is suspended by the following question rather than directly governing ayyuhā.
Al-Ḥasan pronounces the command lām of falyanẓur with kasra; most readers use sukūn.
Azkā means better quality, finer, or more wholesome food.
note: Other glosses emphasize taste, quality, quantity, or price; lawful food may be tied to slaughter or unjust acquisition.

view: Azkā means tastier or more pleasant food.
note: Other glosses emphasize taste, quality, quantity, or price; lawful food may be tied to slaughter or unjust acquisition.

view: Azkā means more abundant food; zakā can denote growth or increase, as an Arabic poem illustrates.
note: Other glosses emphasize taste, quality, quantity, or price; lawful food may be tied to slaughter or unjust acquisition.

view: Azkā means less expensive food.
note: Other glosses emphasize taste, quality, quantity, or price; lawful food may be tied to slaughter or unjust acquisition.

view: Azkā may mean more blessed or fruitful food.
Zakā conveys increase or purification, including increase in goodness, benefit, or spiritual reward.
Ayyuhā is an interrogative subject with azkā as predicate and ṭaʿāman as specification; the question follows the verb of looking.
Ayy may be interrogative or a relative object in Sībawayh's analysis, with a corresponding implied predicate.
“Which of them” means which of the city's inhabitants; the understood word is its people.
“Which of them” may instead refer to foods understood from context, without eliding “people.”
Ayyahā may mean which place or shop within the city offers the best food.
Reports name rice, raisins, or dates as the food the youths sought.
They sought lawful or pure food, especially meat properly slaughtered by believers because idolatrous or Magian townspeople's slaughter was impermissible.
note: Other glosses emphasize taste, quality, quantity, or price; lawful food may be tied to slaughter or unjust acquisition.

view: They sought food free from unjust seizure, theft, or the tyrant's extortion.
note: Other glosses emphasize taste, quality, quantity, or price; lawful food may be tied to slaughter or unjust acquisition.

view: The lawful and pure reading is preferred because good food is desirable regardless of quantity and lawful food outweighs abundant unlawful food.
A reading of azkā as the best or purest quality is preferred, while lawful wholesomeness remains a concern.
Some interpret the food instruction as choosing delicate food after a long fast, since coarse food might harm them.
A suggestion places food conscious People of the Book in Raqīm; careful selection of food could have exposed the envoy.
Buy delicate food for the poor or spiritually knowledgeable, but ascetics can accept whatever is available as discipline.
The purest food symbolizes sound knowledge that nourishes the heart, free of empty disputation and superficial arts.
Al-Ālūsī criticizes accepting money known to come from an oppressor even when it is defended as feeding hungry seekers.
Al-Ālūsī rejects a spiritual rule of delicate food: it can hinder perfection and conflicts with the Prophet's and Companions' simple lives.
Seeking the purest food teaches scrupulousness in nourishment and spiritual life.
Rizq here means food or sustenance to bring back and eat.
The pronoun in rizqan minhu may refer to the selected food or the silver; min may mark a part, source, or substitute.
The pronoun in “from it” most naturally refers to the chosen food; referring it to the silver would require another implicit pronoun.
The command lām in falyatikum can be read with sukūn or its original kasra.
The provision brought back should be lawful to eat.
Once spiritual absorption gave way to discernment, their first concern was food, showing bodily nourishment's priority.
Luṭf can denote smallness, gentleness in action, or God's kindness and mercy.
Ishʿār means informing or making aware, from shaʿara, to perceive or know; related usage includes the word poet.
In the following threat, ẓuhūr may mean discovering their location or gaining power over them.
Another gloss understands the threatened rajm as verbal abuse.
“Return you to their creed” can mean force you to become members of it even without previous membership.
The verb “return into their creed” implies insertion, accounting for the preposition fī rather than ilā.
The warning covers conduct that unintentionally alerts others, since the envoy would cause their awareness.
The omission of what specifically must remain hidden lets the warning cover the youths' existence, number, and location.
The emphatic nūn underscores the danger explained by the following threat.
Al-Ḥasan reads the command lām of walyatalaṭṭaf with its original kasra; most readers use sukūn.
Qutayba al-Mayyāl reads yutalaṭṭaf in the passive with ḍamma on yāʾ.
Some read lā yushʿiranna actively with aḥad as nominative subject.
Zayd b. ʿAlī reads the following yaẓharū verb in the passive.
The subsequent plural pronoun refers to the city's people understood in “which of them.”
A contrary report says the envoy was sworn to lead captors to his companions if captured so all could share martyrdom.
note: This differs from the reading that forbids exposing companions even after capture.

view: Separated from the others, the envoy recalled their pledge never to forsake faith or each other in life or death.
When the envoy delayed and horses approached, the youths feared Deqianus had captured him; they prayed and expected the tyrant.
One calculation places the Qurʾān's midpoint at the word walyatalaṭṭaf; another places it elsewhere in the sūra.
The envoy should act discreetly and carefully while entering town, shopping, traveling, and returning, to avoid recognition.
Talaṭṭuf may require gentle, courteous dealing with the seller so no quarrel draws notice.
Talaṭṭuf may mean bargaining carefully or handling the purchase so he is not cheated.
Talaṭṭuf may mean shopping without contentious haggling or argument.
The author rejects a broad transaction caution as unsupported by the explicit warning that follows.
The envoy must not reveal the youths or their location to anyone in the city.
If the envoy is discovered, he must not expose his companions to danger.
note: A contrary report says captors should be led to the companions so all share martyrdom.

view: Discovery threatened the youths with stoning or forced return to unbelief, destroying their prospect of success.
The threatened rajm most likely means physical stoning, a punishment for dissenters in earlier times.
Entering the persecutors' religion would forfeit success; idhā marks that conditional outcome.
Forced return would involve idolatrous practices and the loss of true worship, beyond verbal assent.
Proposed explanations of forced apostasy through Satanic influence, mere invitation, or a former ban on concealment lack textual support.
A captive or powerless believer may outwardly comply under coercion while keeping inward faith.
A person able to leave who voluntarily enters a hostile society and loses ability to profess faith has wronged himself.
Treat people of spiritual knowledge gently and spiritual novices firmly.
Choose a verified, pure hearted spiritual guide rather than a pretender; companionship yields insight.
The envoy is thought, the city the gathered faculties, and pure food intellect rather than illusion, imagination, or sensation; discretion hides faith from the ignorant.
Secrecy symbolizes concealing spiritual realities from people unable to perceive their light.
